fetched_contents.text: Delving into the role of microwave curing on the strength and cement hydration features of cemented tailings backfill 1. Introduction Cemented tailings backfill (CTB) is a stable blend of mineral tails, binders, and mixing water with liquid quality content typically ranging from 15wt% to 30wt% [1], [2], [3]. After being mixed and stirred evenly, CTB slurries are transported to goaves to control surface subsidence and mitigate safety hazards caused by the surface storage of tailings [4], [5], [6]. Additionally, CTB can replace remaining pillars to support the roof in underground mining operations, thereby achieving a full recovery of resources [7], [8], [9]. Accordingly, rapidly enhancing early-aged backfill strength is substantial in shortening the mining and filling cycle time and improving mining efficiency. In the two-step mining process, CTB is used as the pillar-supporting roof and must thus possess a certain strength. Otherwise, CTB failure can seriously affect safe ore production from underground mines. Therefore, many experts and scholars have explored ways to enhance CTB’s strength, especially for early ages [9], [10], [11], [12]. For instance, Yilmaz et al. [13] designed a pressure-capable curing test device to further explore the effect of different factors (e.g., age and binder) on CTB strength. Meanwhile, Wang et al. [14] discovered the impact of straw on the backfill strength property and explored the mechanisms that emerged from a microstructure perspective. Cao et al. [15], [16] determined that the fiber type strongly affected the strength property of CTB at the early stages of curing. In addition, many studies have shown that CTB strength is sensitive to temperature [17], [18], [19]. The low temperatures of mines located in alpine regions may sizably hinder hydration reactions and affect CTB’s strength [20]. Higher temperatures can accelerate the reaction of cement hydration, resulting in additional hydration products and thus facilitating higher fill strength [21], [22]. Thus, CTB’s strength can be boosted by enhanced temperature conditions. The attention to microwave-curing concrete and geopolymers has increased significantly with the gradual maturity of microwave technology. Microwaves have fast heating speeds and uniform temperatures. In this regard, advanced microwave technologies exhibit promising applications across various domains. In the 1980s and 1990s, many scholars began researching microwave-curing concrete in the civil engineering and construction industry [23], [24], [25]. For instance, Bai et al. [26] anticipated a laboratory technique for the microwave-curing polymer of a high-titanium slag base and verified its feasibility. Tan et al. [27] meaningfully improved the strength property of recycled aggregate geopolymers using microwave technology and experimentally explored the influence of numerous parameters (e.g., microwave curing, elapsed time, metakaolin content, and alkali dosage) on the microwave curing of recycled aggregate geopolymers. Meanwhile, the study of Kong et al. [28] showed that a microwave-cured composite binder can help form dense structures and explored the mechanism of microwave curing. Mangat et al. [29] used microwaves to repair cementitious products such as concrete and discovered a coupling link between microwave power, age, and curing temperature. Concrete, CTB, and geopolymer materials exhibited numerous similarities. Wu et al. [30] and Sun et al. [31], [32] used a domestic microwave oven to treat CTB and verified in a laboratory environment that such microwave treatment can be instrumental in developing relatively high backfill strengths, which verified the feasibility of microwave-curing CTB to improve its early strength. Boosting backfill strength involves hydration reactions. In this respect, CTB’s hydration products can be obtained using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and thermogravimetric/differential thermogravimetric (TG/DTG) experiments. XRD is a powerful method for studying crystal structures [28], [33], [34]. The composition of elements or groups of crystalline substances leads to discrepancies in intensity, angular position, and shape of diffraction peaks [35]. By comparing a specimen’s XRD spectrum with those of already known crystalline materials, its phase and structure can be well obtained [36]. However, hydration products contain amorphous hydrated calcium silicate. In this respect, TG/DTG examines the relationship between the sample quality and temperature or time using a certain heating or cooling rate and can thus detect calcium silicate hydrate [37]. The mass variation and rate of variation can be accurately measured to obtain the physical property change in a sample [38]. Most studies have shown that the strength of concrete/geopolymers is promptly boosted via microwave curing [39], [40], [41]. Thus, a horn microwave device was developed herein to further explore the possibility of conducting a microwave-curing CTB industrial test. The effects of the microwave curing time on upper surface temperature, strength gain/increase, and deformation coefficient of 3- to 28-d-cured CTB specimens were experimentally explored. This investigation revealed the influence of microwave curing time on the hydration mechanism of CTB specimens using XRD and TG/DTG tests, providing a theoretical basis for enhancing early-aged CTB strength through microwave irradiation. fetched_contents.text: Study on strength and durability characteristics of nano-silica based blended concrete 1. Introduction Concrete is the most commonly used materials in the world. The increased demand for cement in concrete by the construction industry is leading to environmental pollution. The construction industry is contributing 5–7% of whole CO2 emissions. The production of cement is the main reason of CO emissions. This is resulting in highly hazardous impact on the environment, and should be minimized these emissions to achieve sustainability. This is mainly due to increasing population in developing countries and the process of undergoing rapid expansion in the infrastructure to meet the increased demand. In order to minimize the amount of CO2 release into the atmosphere, the concept of blended concretes should be incorporated. The economy point of the construction activity can also be addressed using SCMs. The utilization of these materials or the combinations of these materials moreover by products from industries such as ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS), fly ash, Nano-silica and other waste materials create landfill problem and leading to environmental pollution. fetched_contents.text: A Review on the Carbonation and Chloride Penetration Resistance of Structural Lightweight Aggregate Concrete Abstract This paper presents a comprehensive review on structural lightweight aggregate concrete (SLWAC) durability. The main transport properties and degradation mechanisms of reinforced concrete are addressed, namely, carbonation and chloride attack. The influence of the main composition parameters, such as type of aggregate, type of binder and water/binder ratio, as well as the influence of cracking, are also analysed. Finally, the current knowledge of SLWAC’s service life prediction is assessed. Although the knowledge of SLWAC’s durability behaviour is still limited, investigation works performed either in laboratory or in real environments indicate that SLWAC can have similar to better durability performance than normal weight concrete, especially when the same strength level is considered. The importance of the quality of the paste over the characteristics of the lightweight aggregates is highlighted. Durability standardization regarding SLWAC is still insufficient and is one of the main gaps of current knowledge. The objective of this review is to foster a better understanding on the durability and service life prediction of SLWAC, contributing to a greater confidence in using this type of concrete. Keywords: lightweight aggregate concrete, durability, carbonation, chloride ingress, service life 1. Introduction Although structural lightweight aggregate concrete (SLWAC) has been used for more than 2000 years, it only assumed greater relevance in construction in the middle of the twentieth century, especially in solutions where the self-weight is a relevant factor, such as in high-rise buildings, shell and slender structures, long-span bridges and rehabilitation works. Since then, SLWAC has been the subject of ongoing technologic and scientific developments, especially in the last three decades, after the technological development of high-performance concrete, the research and application of new admixtures, the advances in manufacturing new lightweight aggregates (LWA) and, most of all, due to the more exigent durability requirements in marine structures, where SLWAC may double the percentage of load reduction [1,2]. However, despite research efforts, knowledge is still limited, especially when compared to that of normal weight concrete (NWC). On the one hand, the higher production costs, the lower quality of the first generation of SLWAC and the less confidence in its application have hindered its affirmation in construction. On the other hand, SLWAC properties can greatly vary depending on the type of LWA and concrete composition, which makes their characterization more complex [3,4,5]. Regarding the durability behavior of SLWAC, knowledge is even less consolidated. Research carried out in this domain shows that the durability and service life performance of SLWAC are influenced by various factors, such as the type of LWA, concrete composition, exposure and testing conditions, water content and deterioration mechanism [6,7], which make its interpretation and general characterization difficult. Nevertheless, the adequate durability of SLWAC has been proven through the excellent performance evidenced by this material applied in old structures. The vessel production during the world wars, which have been subjected to aggressive environmental conditions for more than a century [1,8,9] evidences the performance of SLWAC in harsh marine environments. The use of SLWAC in the shipbuilding industry was also of great importance in the former Soviet Union. After 15–40 years of navigation experience, no significant corrosion phenomenon was observed [10]. A survey of the Concrete Society [11], which summarizes the use of SLWAC in road structures in North America, the former Soviet Union and Western Europe, indicates that the durability of SLWAC is at least equivalent to NWC. One of the most significant examples of the durability of SLWAC is attributed to the William Preston Lane Jr. Memorial Bridge, built in 1952, over the Chesapeake Bay in Annapolis, Maryland. The suspension span was built with SLWAC of 24 MPa and water/cement ratio (w/c) of 0.4, while the approach spans were built in NWC [12,13]. In 1975, petrographic and ultrasonic analysis, showing the notable integrity of SLWAC and high deterioration of NWC, led to the option of rebuild the NWC spans with SLWAC. Mays and Barnes [14] carried out a comprehensive examination of 40 structures in the United Kingdom, including bridges, parking decks and buildings, which indicated that SLWAC was no less durable than NWC. Thienel et al. [15] also reported good durability against freezing and thawing, carbonation and chloride attack of different types of SLWAC from 15 structures in Germany. Both studies indicate that an eventual poor durability of SLWAC may be related to its production process and greater tendency for aggregate segregation. The durability of SLWAC has also been demonstrated by the Norwegian experience of its application in marine structures, namely, long-span bridges and offshore structures [14,15]. Various investigations on the durability performance of SLWAC in these structures, including laboratory and in-situ tests, suggested that the chloride penetration resistance in SLWAC tends to be at least as high as in NWC [16,17]. However, despite some examples of good performance, knowledge on the durability behavior of SLWAC is still scarce and the mechanisms of deterioration are less dominated than in conventional NWC. Microwave curing improves strength and durability primarily by accelerating hydration and modifying microstructure, but its effects are context-dependent and can be influenced by CFA-specific behavior.

First, microwave curing accelerates hydration and reduces early-age defects. The evidence from the microwave curing literature shows that microwave energy can accelerate cement hydration and increase early-age strength, partly because of its fast heating and uniform temperature characteristics [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In concrete and related materials, higher temperatures are generally associated with faster hydration reactions and higher early-age strength, with microwave curing being positioned as a promising method to shorten curing times [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The cited review on CTB also emphasizes that microwave treatment can be instrumental in developing relatively high backfill strengths, and that it can be used to explore hydration mechanisms [N1-F1]. Although the evidence here is not a direct “early-age defect” mechanism, the overall logic is that accelerated hydration reduces the window during which unhydrated cement paste is vulnerable to cracking, segregation, or other early-age defects.

Second, microwave curing modifies microstructure and pore distribution. The evidence supports that microwave curing can lead to denser structures and can influence hydration products and pore structure [N1-F1]. The same source also indicates that microwave curing was used to explore the hydration mechanism of CTB specimens using XRD and TG/DTG tests, implying that pore and hydrate distributions are measurable and responsive to curing conditions [N1-F1]. While the evidence is indirect for CFA-specific microstructure, the general principle is that microwave curing can refine microstructure by promoting earlier and more uniform hydration, which is consistent with how microwave curing is described in the broader cement-based materials literature [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. This is important because denser microstructures are linked to lower permeability and better durability.

Third, the durability properties improved by microwave curing depend on the specific exposure and conditions. The evidence here is strongest for early-age performance, with microwave curing linked to improved early strength and early hydration [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1]. However, the durability-related evidence provided in the current dependencies is less specific. The CFA durability context does indicate that low water-cement ratio, high pozzolan or slag content, and adequate concrete quality can improve durability [N5-R3], but this is general concrete context rather than a direct statement about microwave curing. Therefore, the durability benefits of microwave curing are likely most evident in early-age performance and in properties that depend on microstructure refinement, such as reduced permeability and improved bonding, rather than in a fully characterized durability profile. The evidence does not strongly indicate that microwave curing consistently improves all durability properties under all conditions, so its durability benefits should be understood as conditional on curing time, temperature, and mix design.

Fourth, CFA-specific properties can affect microwave curing outcomes. The CFA context shows that CFA concretes can have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. In particular, the evidence suggests that CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5], which is consistent with the general idea that CFA improves durability through pore refinement and additional hydration products. However, the evidence also suggests that CFA concretes may have some limitations: for example, one CFA study found that at 30% CFA, ordinary concrete showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete, while another source notes that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems [N6-R4][N6-R1]. This matters because microwave curing may be more effective in mixes with lower initial porosity and better initial hydration, whereas CFA mixes may require careful calibration to balance early hydration gains with longer-term performance. The CFA-specific behavior is therefore not inherently incompatible with microwave curing, but the curing response may depend on the mix’s baseline porosity, cement content, and exposure conditions.

Overall, microwave curing improves strength and durability mainly by accelerating hydration and refining microstructure, but its durability benefits are most clearly supported in early-age and microstructure-related properties. CFA-specific properties can either complement or complicate these effects, depending on the mix’s baseline porosity, water absorption, and long-term hydration behavior [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5].

Nanosilica improves strength and durability primarily through its high pozzolanic activity and pore-refining filler effect, which together enhance strength gain and reduce permeability, but its effectiveness can be modified by CFA-specific behavior.

First, nanosilica contributes to pozzolanic reaction and strength gain. The evidence is explicit: nano-silica has very high pozzolanic activity and its filling effect notably influences pore structure refinement [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. It also acts as a pozzolanic material with dual effects, enhancing nucleation and performance characteristics through both filler and pozzolanic reaction [N2-F2]. This dual mechanism is important because the pozzolanic reaction produces additional C–S–H gel, which can fill pores and improve strength, while the filler effect reduces porosity by occupying void space [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2]. The same evidence base also states that the pozzolanic activity and filler effect contribute to pore structure refinement, reinforcing the idea that strength gain is not just a matter of faster hydration but also of microstructure evolution [N2-R3][N2-F2].

Second, nanosilica refines pore structure and reduces permeability. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that nanosilica filling notably influences pore structure refinement and that durability properties are affected by this [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. It also states that nanosilica improves durability and mechanical performances of OPC concrete, which is consistent with reduced permeability [N2-F2]. The broader pozzolanic context in the same source further notes that mineral admixtures improve concrete performance, corrosion resistance, high strength, enhanced durability, and low permeability [N2-F2]. So the main durability benefit of nanosilica is a more refined pore structure, which lowers permeability and makes the material less susceptible to ingress of water, ions, or gases.

Third, the durability effects supported by evidence include improved strength and durability, particularly in cementitious systems. The evidence base supports that nanosilica-based blended concrete improves strength and durability characteristics [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The same source also notes that mineral admixtures improve concrete performance in aggressive environments and enhance durability [N2-F2]. While the evidence does not provide a comprehensive durability profile for all properties, it does strongly support chloride and carbonation resistance-like benefits through pore refinement and pozzolanic reaction, as well as general durability improvement [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The evidence here is less explicit than the microwave curing evidence on exact durability properties, but the logic is consistent: a denser, more refined microstructure should improve resistance to transport processes that depend on porosity, such as carbonation and chloride penetration.

Fourth, CFA-specific behavior can change nanosilica effectiveness. The CFA context suggests that CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5], but also that CFA concretes may have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. In particular, one CFA study found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems, and another found that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R1][N6-R4]. This matters because nanosilica effectiveness depends on the initial porosity and hydration state of the mix. If CFA already lowers permeability and improves long-term durability, nanosilica may add only incremental benefits, or it may be more effective if the CFA mix has residual porosity that nanosilica can refine further [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5]. However, the evidence does not show a direct conflict; rather, CFA and nanosilica may work in the same direction, but the degree of benefit depends on the baseline mix behavior.

In summary, nanosilica improves strength and durability mainly by high pozzolanic activity and pore-refining filler effects, reducing permeability and improving strength gain [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2]. Its durability benefits are most clearly supported in transport-resistance and microstructure-related properties, but CFA-specific behavior may amplify or modulate these effects depending on the mix’s baseline porosity and hydration response [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5].

Metakaolin improves strength and durability mainly through pozzolanic activity and microstructure refinement, but it differs from nanosilica in behavior and effectiveness, and its performance can be influenced by CFA-specific behavior.

First, metakaolin contributes to pozzolanic activity and strength development. The evidence indicates that metakaolin is a pozzolanic material whose hydration and pozzolanic reaction can be coupled during early stages [N3-R1]. It also suggests that the incorporation of metakaolin into cementitious materials can improve compressive strength and durability [N3-R3]. The same source further states that adding metakaolin to concrete enhances certain characteristics, particularly mechanical capabilities, although it decreases concrete flowability [N3-R4]. This shows that metakaolin’s main strength-related contribution is not just increased hydration rate but also the formation of pozzolanic products that strengthen the matrix over time.

CFA’s properties interact with additives and microwave curing. CFA’s pozzolanic and permeability-reducing properties make it compatible with additives like nanosilica and metakaolin, which also refine pore structure and improve durability [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. This means that microwave curing and additives can amplify CFA’s benefits by improving hydration and microstructure. On the limitation side, CFA-specific behavior can complicate the response. The upstream aggregates indicate that CFA concretes may have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. Some CFA studies found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption, and that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R1][N6-R4]. These results imply that CFA mixes may retain some weaknesses, such as higher initial porosity, different hydration kinetics, or greater susceptibility to early-age transport processes [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5]. Therefore, microwave curing and additives may be more effective in CFA cement when they are used to address these baseline weaknesses, but the exact degree of improvement depends on mix design, exposure, and curing conditions [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].

---

## 6) Bottom line

In short, microwave curing and additives such as nanosilica and metakaolin improve CFA cement by working together in a complementary way:

- **Microwave curing** accelerates hydration, reduces early-age defects, and modifies microstructure [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3].
- **Nanosilica** contributes high pozzolanic activity and pore-refining filler effects, improving strength and reducing permeability [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2].
- **Metakaolin** contributes pozzolanic activity and microstructure refinement, improving compressive strength and long-term durability, but with a more flowability penalty than nanosilica [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].
- The **best combination** is usually nanosilica with metakaolin, because they combine early-age hydration acceleration with pore refinement and long-term strength gain [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4].
- **CFA-specific effects** can amplify or complicate these benefits: CFA can improve long-term strength and durability, but it can also have different hydration, porosity, and durability behavior, including some limitations such as water absorption and early carbonation [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Overall, the most effective strategy for CFA cement is to use microwave curing and nano-additives together, especially nanosilica with metakaolin, to maximize early-age strength, microstructure refinement, and long-term durability, while carefully managing CFA-specific weaknesses [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Microwave curing improves strength and durability primarily by accelerating hydration and modifying microstructure, but its effects are context-dependent and can be influenced by CFA-specific behavior.

First, microwave curing accelerates hydration and reduces early-age defects. The evidence from the microwave curing literature shows that microwave energy can accelerate cement hydration and increase early-age strength, partly because of its fast heating and uniform temperature characteristics [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In concrete and related materials, higher temperatures are generally associated with faster hydration reactions and higher early-age strength, with microwave curing being positioned as a promising method to shorten curing times [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The cited review on CTB also emphasizes that microwave treatment can be instrumental in developing relatively high backfill strengths, and that it can be used to explore hydration mechanisms [N1-F1]. Although the evidence here is not a direct “early-age defect” mechanism, the overall logic is that accelerated hydration reduces the window during which unhydrated cement paste is vulnerable to cracking, segregation, or other early-age defects.

Second, microwave curing modifies microstructure and pore distribution. The evidence supports that microwave curing can lead to denser structures and can influence hydration products and pore structure [N1-F1]. The same source also indicates that microwave curing was used to explore the hydration mechanism of CTB specimens using XRD and TG/DTG tests, implying that pore and hydrate distributions are measurable and responsive to curing conditions [N1-F1]. While the evidence is indirect for CFA-specific microstructure, the general principle is that microwave curing can refine microstructure by promoting earlier and more uniform hydration, which is consistent with how microwave curing is described in the broader cement-based materials literature [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. This is important because denser microstructures are linked to lower permeability and better durability.

Third, the durability properties improved by microwave curing depend on the specific exposure and conditions. The evidence here is strongest for early-age performance, with microwave curing linked to improved early strength and early hydration [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1]. However, the durability-related evidence provided in the current dependencies is less specific. The CFA durability context does indicate that low water-cement ratio, high pozzolan or slag content, and adequate concrete quality can improve durability [N5-R3], but this is general concrete context rather than a direct statement about microwave curing. Therefore, the durability benefits of microwave curing are likely most evident in early-age performance and in properties that depend on microstructure refinement, such as reduced permeability and improved bonding, rather than in a fully characterized durability profile. The evidence does not strongly indicate that microwave curing consistently improves all durability properties under all conditions, so its durability benefits should be understood as conditional on curing time, temperature, and mix design.

Fourth, CFA-specific properties can affect microwave curing outcomes. The CFA context shows that CFA concretes can have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. In particular, the evidence suggests that CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5], which is consistent with the general idea that CFA improves durability through pore refinement and additional hydration products. However, the evidence also suggests that CFA concretes may have some limitations: for example, one CFA study found that at 30% CFA, ordinary concrete showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete, while another source notes that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems [N6-R4][N6-R1]. This matters because microwave curing may be more effective in mixes with lower initial porosity and better initial hydration, whereas CFA mixes may require careful calibration to balance early hydration gains with longer-term performance. The CFA-specific behavior is therefore not inherently incompatible with microwave curing, but the curing response may depend on the mix’s baseline porosity, cement content, and exposure conditions.

Overall, microwave curing improves strength and durability mainly by accelerating hydration and refining microstructure, but its durability benefits are most clearly supported in early-age and microstructure-related properties. CFA-specific properties can either complement or complicate these effects, depending on the mix’s baseline porosity, water absorption, and long-term hydration behavior [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5].

First, nanosilica contributes to pozzolanic reaction and strength gain. The evidence is explicit: nano-silica has very high pozzolanic activity and its filling effect notably influences pore structure refinement [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. It also acts as a pozzolanic material with dual effects, enhancing nucleation and performance characteristics through both filler and pozzolanic reaction [N2-F2]. This dual mechanism is important because the pozzolanic reaction produces additional C–S–H gel, which can fill pores and improve strength, while the filler effect reduces porosity by occupying void space [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2]. The same evidence base also states that the pozzolanic activity and filler effect contribute to pore structure refinement, reinforcing the idea that strength gain is not just a matter of faster hydration but also of microstructure evolution [N2-R3][N2-F2].

Second, nanosilica refines pore structure and reduces permeability. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that nanosilica filling notably influences pore structure refinement and that durability properties are affected by this [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. Second, CFA affects chloride, sulfate, and carbonation resistance. The evidence supports that ternary cements made with GBFS and/or CFA presented better chloride diffusion resistance than plain Portland cement concrete [N7-R1]. It also states that CFA concretes may have different sulfate and carbonation resistance because of changes in porosity and hydration [N6-R4][N6-R5]. ## 1) How microwave curing improves strength and durability

Microwave curing improves strength and durability mainly by accelerating hydration and reducing early-age defects. The evidence shows that microwave energy can accelerate cement hydration, increase early-age strength, and promote faster reaction kinetics [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3]. In concrete and related materials, higher temperatures are associated with faster hydration reactions and higher early-age strength, with microwave curing positioned as a promising method to shorten curing times [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The cited review on cemented tailings backfill also emphasizes that microwave treatment can be instrumental in developing relatively high backfill strengths and that it can be used to explore hydration mechanisms [N1-F1]. This means microwave curing can reduce the window during which unhydrated cement paste is vulnerable to cracking, segregation, or other early-age defects.

Microwave curing also modifies microstructure and pore distribution. The evidence supports that microwave curing can lead to denser structures and can influence hydration products and pore structure [N1-F1]. The same source also indicates that microwave curing was used to explore the hydration mechanism of CTB specimens using XRD and TG/DTG tests, implying that pore and hydrate distributions are measurable and responsive to curing conditions [N1-F1]. The general principle is that microwave curing promotes earlier and more uniform hydration, which is consistent with how microwave curing is described in the broader cement-based materials literature [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. This is important because denser microstructures are linked to lower permeability and better durability.

The durability properties improved by microwave curing depend on the specific exposure and conditions. The evidence here is strongest for early-age performance, with microwave curing linked to improved early strength and early hydration [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1]. However, the durability-related evidence is less specific in the current dependencies, so the durability benefits are most clearly supported in early-age and microstructure-related properties rather than in a fully characterized durability profile [N5-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5]. Therefore, microwave curing is especially valuable in mixes where early-age strength and microstructure refinement are critical.

CFA-specific properties can affect microwave curing outcomes. CFA concretes may have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. Some CFA studies found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption, and that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R1][N6-R4]. This matters because microwave curing may be more effective in mixes with lower initial porosity and better initial hydration, whereas CFA mixes may require careful calibration to balance early hydration gains with longer-term performance. Overall, microwave curing tends to improve strength and durability, but its effects are context-dependent and can be influenced by CFA-specific behavior [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5].

## 2) How nanosilica improves strength and durability

Nanosilica improves strength and durability primarily through its high pozzolanic activity and pore-refining filler effect. The evidence is explicit: nano-silica has very high pozzolanic activity, and its filling effect notably influences pore structure refinement [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. It also acts as a pozzolanic material with dual effects, enhancing nucleation and performance characteristics through both filler and pozzolanic reaction [N2-F2]. This dual mechanism is important because the pozzolanic reaction produces additional C–S–H gel, which can fill pores and improve strength, while the filler effect reduces porosity by occupying void space [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2]. The same evidence base also states that the pozzolanic activity and filler effect contribute to pore structure refinement, reinforcing the idea that strength gain is not just a matter of faster hydration but also of microstructure evolution [N2-R3][N2-F2].

Nanosilica refines pore structure and reduces permeability. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that nanosilica filling notably influences pore structure refinement and that durability properties are affected by this [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. It also states that nanosilica improves durability and mechanical performances of OPC concrete, which is consistent with reduced permeability [N2-F2]. The broader pozzolanic context in the same source further notes that mineral admixtures improve concrete performance, corrosion resistance, high strength, enhanced durability, and low permeability [N2-F2]. So the main durability benefit of nanosilica is a more refined pore structure, which lowers permeability and makes the material less susceptible to ingress of water, ions, or gases.

The durability effects supported by evidence include improved strength and durability, particularly in cementitious systems. The evidence base supports that nanosilica-based blended concrete improves strength and durability characteristics [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The same source also notes that mineral admixtures improve concrete performance in aggressive environments and enhance durability [N2-F2]. While the evidence does not provide a comprehensive durability profile for all properties, it does strongly support chloride and carbonation resistance-like benefits through pore refinement and pozzolanic reaction, as well as general durability improvement [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The evidence here is less explicit than the microwave curing evidence on exact durability properties, but the logic is consistent: a denser, more refined microstructure should improve resistance to transport processes that depend on porosity, such as carbonation and chloride penetration.

CFA-specific behavior can change nanosilica effectiveness. CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5], but it can also have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. In particular, one CFA study found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems, and another found that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R1][N6-R4]. This matters because nanosilica effectiveness depends on the initial porosity and hydration state of the mix. If CFA already lowers permeability and improves long-term durability, nanosilica may add only incremental benefits, or it may be more effective if the CFA mix has residual porosity that nanosilica can refine further [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5]. However, the evidence does not show a direct conflict; rather, CFA and nanosilica may work in the same direction, but the degree of benefit depends on the baseline mix behavior.

---

## 3) How metakaolin improves strength and durability

Metakaolin improves strength and durability mainly through pozzolanic activity and microstructure refinement. The evidence indicates that metakaolin is a pozzolanic material whose hydration and pozzolanic reaction can be coupled during the early stage [N3-R1]. It also suggests that the incorporation of metakaolin into cementitious materials can improve compressive strength and durability [N3-R3]. The same source further states that adding metakaolin to concrete enhances certain characteristics, particularly mechanical capabilities, although it decreases concrete flowability [N3-R4]. This shows that metakaolin’s main strength-related contribution is not just increased hydration rate but also the formation of pozzolanic products that strengthen the matrix over time.

Metakaolin affects microstructure and long-term durability. The evidence supports that metakaolin can improve compressive strength and durability, which are correlated well with microstructure development [N3-R3]. It also implies that metakaolin can influence the physical properties and long-term performance of concrete made with metakaolin as a binder [N3-R2]. The broader context in the same dependency set suggests that metakaolin concrete improves engineering properties, including durability [N3-R5]. While the evidence is not as detailed as for nanosilica, it is clear that metakaolin acts through microstructural refinement and long-term strength development, rather than just early hydration acceleration.

Metakaolin differs from nanosilica in behavior and effectiveness. The main difference is that nanosilica is characterized as a highly pozzolanic material with a strong filling effect and dual effects on nucleation and performance, whereas metakaolin is described as a binder whose hydration and pozzolanic reaction are coupled, and whose addition improves mechanical capabilities but reduces flowability [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. Nanosilica’s evidence emphasizes pore structure refinement and a broad durability benefit, whereas metakaolin’s evidence emphasizes compressive strength and durability linked to microstructure and long-term performance, with a more flowability penalty [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. In practical terms, nanosilica is often preferred where high early strength and extreme durability are needed, while metakaolin is useful for long-term strength and durability but may require more careful handling of workability.

CFA-specific behavior can change metakaolin effectiveness. CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5], but it can also have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. In particular, one CFA study found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems, and another found that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R1][N6-R4]. This matters because metakaolin effectiveness depends on the initial porosity and hydration state of the mix. If CFA already lowers permeability and improves long-term durability, metakaolin may add only incremental benefits, or it may be more effective if the CFA mix has residual porosity that metakaolin can refine further [N3-R3][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5]. However, the evidence does not show a direct conflict; rather, metakaolin and CFA may work in the same direction, but the degree of benefit depends on the baseline mix behavior.

## 4) Combined effects of microwave curing and nano-additives

The combined effects of microwave curing and nano-additives on CFA cement are generally synergistic, with microwave curing often enhancing additive benefits, improving compressive strength and durability, and the most effective combinations being those that combine early-age hydration acceleration with pore refinement [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3][N8-R2][N4-R5].

Microwave curing often enhances or preserves additive benefits rather than diminishing them. The evidence on microwave curing shows that microwave treatment can accelerate hydration and improve early-age strength, with higher temperatures associated with faster hydration reactions and higher early-age strength [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3]. In the microwave-specific evidence, microwave curing was also described as offsetting early-age strength deficiency in MK mortars and improving 28-day strength [N8-R2]. This is important because many additives, especially pozzolanic ones like nanosilica and metakaolin, may not fully realize their benefits without sufficient hydration and microstructure refinement. The evidence also suggests that appropriately controlled microwave curing provides concurrent improvements in strength, durability-related properties, and sustainability [N4-R5]. So, in most cases, microwave curing appears to support additive performance rather than reduce it.

The combination affects compressive strength and durability positively. The synergy evidence is strongest for nanosilica and metakaolin together. One study found that using metakaolin waste and nano-silica together significantly enhanced the long-term strength of concrete, with the mix showing improved mechanical properties after 2 years [N4-R1]. Another study reported concrete samples with 28-day strengths of 31.5 MPa, 5.7 MPa splitting tensile strength, and 10.6 MPa flexural strength when metakaolin and silica fume were used together [N4-R2]. A third source described geopolymer concrete specimens substituted with 10% metakaolin and 3% nano-silica as having better mechanical properties and improved pore structure observations [N4-R3]. These results indicate that the combination can improve compressive strength, flexural strength, and durability-related microstructure.

The durability benefit is also supported by microstructure evidence. The same synergy evidence notes that modified metakaolin with nano-silica improves mechanical properties and durability [N4-R4]. Additionally, the broader pozzolanic evidence in the upstream aggregates indicates that nanosilica refines pore structure, reduces permeability, and improves durability [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2]. Metakaolin also improves compressive strength and durability, with microstructure refinement and long-term performance being central to its effect [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. In combination, microwave curing, nanosilica, and metakaolin therefore work through complementary mechanisms: microwave curing accelerates hydration and reduces early-age defects, while the additives refine microstructure and pore structure, together improving both compressive strength and durability [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3][N8-R2][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].

Which additive combinations are most effective and why depends on the synergy between pozzolanic and hydration acceleration. The most effective combinations appear to be metakaolin with nano-silica, because they combine early-age hydration acceleration with pore refinement and long-term strength gain [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence also suggests that microwave curing can be especially beneficial when paired with additives that improve microstructure, because it helps offset early-age strength deficiencies and enhances the durability-related properties that additives alone may not fully activate [N8-R2][N4-R5]. The reason these combinations are effective is that nanosilica and metakaolin both contribute pozzolanic activity and pore refinement, while microwave curing improves hydration kinetics and microstructure development [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4][N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3]. The best combinations are therefore those where the additives are used to refine the microstructure, and microwave curing is used to ensure sufficient hydration and early-age performance.

## 5) CFA-specific durability and how CFA affects performance

CFA-specific durability and performance are shaped by hydration, porosity, long-term strength, and interactions with additives and curing conditions. The evidence shows that CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5]. It also indicates that CFA concretes may have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. Some CFA studies found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption, and that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R1][N6-R4]. These results suggest that CFA does not always behave as a universal strength booster; instead, its effects depend on how well hydration is controlled and how porosity is distributed [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5].

CFA affects chloride, sulfate, and carbonation resistance. The evidence supports that ternary cements made with GBFS and/or CFA presented better chloride diffusion resistance than plain Portland cement concrete [N7-R1]. It also states that CFA concretes may have different sulfate and carbonation resistance because of changes in porosity and hydration [N6-R4][N6-R5]. The durability review on carbonation and chloride penetration resistance in concrete emphasizes that low water-cement ratio, high pozzolan or slag content, and adequate concrete quality can improve durability [N5-R3]. This aligns with the CFA context: because CFA is a pozzolanic material, it can reduce permeability and improve chloride and sulfate resistance by refining the pore system [N7-R5][N7-R1]. However, the evidence also shows that CFA concretes may still be vulnerable to some transport phenomena, such as higher early carbonation or greater water absorption [N6-R1][N6-R4], so durability is not guaranteed simply by the presence of CFA.

CFA-related limitations remain despite additive or curing improvements. The evidence indicates that CFA concretes may still have limitations. For example, one study found that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R4]. Another found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems [N6-R1]. These results suggest that even with additives or improved curing, CFA mixes may retain some weaknesses, such as higher initial porosity, different hydration kinetics, or greater susceptibility to early-age transport processes [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5]. The evidence also suggests that CFA’s durability benefits may be conditional on mix design, exposure, and curing conditions rather than automatic [N5-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5].

CFA’s properties interact with additives and microwave curing. CFA’s pozzolanic and permeability-reducing properties make it compatible with additives like nanosilica and metakaolin, which also refine pore structure and improve durability [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. This means that microwave curing and additives can amplify CFA’s benefits by improving hydration and microstructure. On the limitation side, CFA-specific behavior can complicate the response. The upstream aggregates indicate that CFA concretes may have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. Some CFA studies found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption, and that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R1][N6-R4]. These results imply that CFA mixes may retain some weaknesses, such as higher initial porosity, different hydration kinetics, or greater susceptibility to early-age transport processes [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5]. Therefore, microwave curing and additives may be more effective in CFA cement when they are used to address these baseline weaknesses, but the exact degree of improvement depends on mix design, exposure, and curing conditions [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].

---

## 6) Bottom line

In short, microwave curing and additives such as nanosilica and metakaolin improve CFA cement by working together in a complementary way:

- **Microwave curing** accelerates hydration, reduces early-age defects, and modifies microstructure [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3].
- **Nanosilica** contributes high pozzolanic activity and pore-refining filler effects, improving strength and reducing permeability [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2].
- **Metakaolin** contributes pozzolanic activity and microstructure refinement, improving compressive strength and long-term durability, but with a more flowability penalty than nanosilica [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].
- The **best combination** is usually nanosilica with metakaolin, because they combine early-age hydration acceleration with pore refinement and long-term strength gain [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4].
- **CFA-specific effects** can amplify or complicate these benefits: CFA can improve long-term strength and durability, but it can also have different hydration, porosity, and durability behavior, including some limitations such as water absorption and early carbonation [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Overall, the most effective strategy for CFA cement is to use microwave curing and nano-additives together, especially nanosilica with metakaolin, to maximize early-age strength, microstructure refinement, and long-term durability, while carefully managing CFA-specific weaknesses [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Microwave curing improves strength and durability primarily by accelerating hydration and modifying microstructure, but its effects are context-dependent and can be influenced by CFA-specific behavior.

First, microwave curing accelerates hydration and reduces early-age defects. The evidence from the microwave curing literature shows that microwave energy can accelerate cement hydration and increase early-age strength, partly because of its fast heating and uniform temperature characteristics [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In concrete and related materials, higher temperatures are generally associated with faster hydration reactions and higher early-age strength, with microwave curing being positioned as a promising method to shorten curing times [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The cited review on CTB also emphasizes that microwave treatment can be instrumental in developing relatively high backfill strengths, and that it can be used to explore hydration mechanisms [N1-F1]. Although the evidence here is not a direct “early-age defect” mechanism, the overall logic is that accelerated hydration reduces the window during which unhydrated cement paste is vulnerable to cracking, segregation, or other early-age defects.

Second, microwave curing modifies microstructure and pore distribution. The evidence supports that microwave curing can lead to denser structures and can influence hydration products and pore structure [N1-F1]. The same source also indicates that microwave curing was used to explore the hydration mechanism of CTB specimens using XRD and TG/DTG tests, implying that pore and hydrate distributions are measurable and responsive to curing conditions [N1-F1]. While the evidence is indirect for CFA-specific microstructure, the general principle is that microwave curing can refine microstructure by promoting earlier and more uniform hydration, which is consistent with how microwave curing is described in the broader cement-based materials literature [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. This is important because denser microstructures are linked to lower permeability and better durability.

Third, the durability properties improved by microwave curing depend on the specific exposure and conditions. The evidence here is strongest for early-age performance, with microwave curing linked to improved early strength and early hydration [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1]. However, the durability-related evidence provided in the current dependencies is less specific. The CFA durability context does indicate that low water-cement ratio, high pozzolan or slag content, and adequate concrete quality can improve durability [N5-R3], but this is general concrete context rather than a direct statement about microwave curing. Therefore, the durability benefits of microwave curing are likely most evident in early-age performance and in properties that depend on microstructure refinement, such as reduced permeability and improved bonding, rather than in a fully characterized durability profile. The evidence does not strongly indicate that microwave curing consistently improves all durability properties under all conditions, so its durability benefits should be understood as conditional on curing time, temperature, and mix design.

Fourth, CFA-specific properties can affect microwave curing outcomes. The CFA context shows that CFA concretes can have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. In particular, the evidence suggests that CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5], which is consistent with the general idea that CFA improves durability through pore refinement and additional hydration products. However, the evidence also suggests that CFA concretes may have some limitations: for example, one CFA study found that at 30% CFA, ordinary concrete showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete, while another source notes that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems [N6-R4][N6-R1]. This matters because microwave curing may be more effective in mixes with lower initial porosity and better initial hydration, whereas CFA mixes may require careful calibration to balance early hydration gains with longer-term performance. The CFA-specific behavior is therefore not inherently incompatible with microwave curing, but the curing response may depend on the mix’s baseline porosity, cement content, and exposure conditions.

Overall, microwave curing improves strength and durability mainly by accelerating hydration and refining microstructure, but its durability benefits are most clearly supported in early-age and microstructure-related properties. CFA-specific properties can either complement or complicate these effects, depending on the mix’s baseline porosity, water absorption, and long-term hydration behavior [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5].

Nanosilica improves strength and durability primarily through its high pozzolanic activity and pore-refining filler effect, which together enhance strength gain and reduce permeability, but its effectiveness can be modified by CFA-specific behavior.

First, nanosilica contributes to pozzolanic reaction and strength gain. The evidence is explicit: nano-silica has very high pozzolanic activity and its filling effect notably influences pore structure refinement [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. It also acts as a pozzolanic material with dual effects, enhancing nucleation and performance characteristics through both filler and pozzolanic reaction [N2-F2]. This dual mechanism is important because the pozzolanic reaction produces additional C–S–H gel, which can fill pores and improve strength, while the filler effect reduces porosity by occupying void space [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2]. The same evidence base also states that the pozzolanic activity and filler effect contribute to pore structure refinement, reinforcing the idea that strength gain is not just a matter of faster hydration but also of microstructure evolution [N2-R3][N2-F2].

Second, nanosilica refines pore structure and reduces permeability. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that nanosilica filling notably influences pore structure refinement and that durability properties are affected by this [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5]. It also states that nanosilica improves durability and mechanical performances of OPC concrete, which is consistent with reduced permeability [N2-F2]. The broader pozzolanic context in the same source further notes that mineral admixtures improve concrete performance, corrosion resistance, high strength, enhanced durability, and low permeability [N2-F2]. So the main durability benefit of nanosilica is a more refined pore structure, which lowers permeability and makes the material less susceptible to ingress of water, ions, or gases.

Third, the durability effects supported by evidence include improved strength and durability, particularly in cementitious systems. The evidence base supports that nanosilica-based blended concrete improves strength and durability characteristics [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The same source also notes that mineral admixtures improve concrete performance in aggressive environments and enhance durability [N2-F2]. While the evidence does not provide a comprehensive durability profile for all properties, it does strongly support chloride and carbonation resistance-like benefits through pore refinement and pozzolanic reaction, as well as general durability improvement [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The evidence here is less explicit than the microwave curing evidence on exact durability properties, but the logic is consistent: a denser, more refined microstructure should improve resistance to transport processes that depend on porosity, such as carbonation and chloride penetration.

Fourth, CFA-specific behavior can change nanosilica effectiveness. The CFA context suggests that CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5], but also that CFA concretes may have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. In particular, one CFA study found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems, and another found that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R1][N6-R4]. This matters because nanosilica effectiveness depends on the initial porosity and hydration state of the mix. If CFA already lowers permeability and improves long-term durability, nanosilica may add only incremental benefits, or it may be more effective if the CFA mix has residual porosity that nanosilica can refine further [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5]. However, the evidence does not show a direct conflict; rather, CFA and nanosilica may work in the same direction, but the degree of benefit depends on the baseline mix behavior.

In summary, nanosilica improves strength and durability mainly by high pozzolanic activity and pore-refining filler effects, reducing permeability and improving strength gain [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2]. Its durability benefits are most clearly supported in transport-resistance and microstructure-related properties, but CFA-specific behavior may amplify or modulate these effects depending on the mix’s baseline porosity and hydration response [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5].

Metakaolin improves strength and durability mainly through pozzolanic activity and microstructure refinement, but it differs from nanosilica in behavior and effectiveness, and its performance can be influenced by CFA-specific behavior.

First, metakaolin contributes to pozzolanic activity and strength development. The evidence indicates that metakaolin is a pozzolanic material whose hydration and pozzolanic reaction can be coupled during early stages [N3-R1]. It also suggests that the incorporation of metakaolin into cementitious materials can improve compressive strength and durability [N3-R3]. The same source further states that adding metakaolin to concrete enhances certain characteristics, particularly mechanical capabilities, although it decreases concrete flowability [N3-R4]. This shows that metakaolin’s main strength-related contribution is not just increased hydration rate but also the formation of pozzolanic products that strengthen the matrix over time.

Second, metakaolin affects microstructure and long-term durability. The evidence supports that metakaolin can improve compressive strength and durability, which are correlated well with microstructure development [N3-R3]. It also implies that metakaolin can influence the physical properties and long-term performance of concrete made with metakaolin as a binder [N3-R2]. The broader context in the same dependency set suggests that metakaolin concrete improves engineering properties, including durability [N3-R5]. While the evidence is not as detailed as for nanosilica, it is clear that metakaolin acts through microstructural refinement and long-term strength development, rather than just early hydration acceleration.

Third, metakaolin differs from nanosilica in behavior and effectiveness. The main difference is that nanosilica is characterized as a highly pozzolanic material with a strong filling effect and dual effects on nucleation and performance, whereas metakaolin is described as a binder whose hydration and pozzolanic reaction are coupled, and whose addition improves mechanical capabilities but reduces flowability [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. Nanosilica’s evidence emphasizes pore structure refinement and a broad durability benefit, whereas metakaolin’s evidence emphasizes compressive strength and durability linked to microstructure and long-term performance, with a more flowability penalty [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. In practical terms, nanosilica is often preferred where high early strength and extreme durability are needed, while metakaolin is useful for long-term strength and durability but may require more careful handling of workability.

Fourth, CFA-specific behavior can change metakaolin effectiveness. The CFA context shows that CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5], but also that CFA concretes may have different hydration, porosity, and long-term strength behavior compared to conventional concrete [N6-R1][N6-R5][N7-R5]. In particular, one CFA study found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems, and another found that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R1][N6-R4]. This matters because metakaolin effectiveness depends on the initial porosity and hydration state of the mix. If CFA already lowers permeability and improves long-term durability, metakaolin may add only incremental benefits, or it may be more effective if the CFA mix has residual porosity that metakaolin can refine further [N3-R3][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5]. However, the evidence does not show a direct conflict; rather, metakaolin and CFA may work in the same direction, but the degree of benefit depends on the baseline mix behavior.

Compared to nanosilica, it behaves differently because it couples hydration and pozzolanic reaction and can reduce flowability, while nanosilica is more focused on pore refinement and broader durability benefits [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2]. CFA-specific durability and performance are shaped by hydration, porosity, long-term strength, and interactions with additives and curing conditions.

First, CFA influences hydration, porosity, and long-term strength. The evidence indicates that CFA can enhance long-term strength and durability while reducing permeability [N7-R5]. Specifically, one CFA study found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems [N6-R1], suggesting that hydration is not always uniform and that porosity can affect strength development. Another source found that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete, indicating that CFA can alter porosity and transport properties even when it improves long-term strength [N6-R4]. This means CFA does not always behave as a universal strength booster; instead, its effects depend on how well hydration is controlled and how porosity is distributed.

Second, CFA affects chloride, sulfate, and carbonation resistance. The evidence supports that ternary cements made with GBFS and/or CFA presented better chloride diffusion resistance than plain Portland cement concrete [N7-R1]. It also states that CFA concretes may have different sulfate and carbonation resistance because of changes in porosity and hydration [N6-R4][N6-R5]. The durability review on carbonation and chloride penetration resistance in concrete emphasizes that low water-cement ratio, high pozzolan or slag content, and adequate concrete quality can improve durability [N5-R3]. This aligns with the CFA context: because CFA is a pozzolanic material, it can reduce permeability and improve chloride and sulfate resistance by refining the pore system [N7-R5][N7-R1]. However, the evidence also shows that CFA concretes may still be vulnerable to some transport phenomena, such as higher early carbonation or greater water absorption [N6-R1][N6-R4], so durability is not guaranteed simply by the presence of CFA.

Third, CFA-related limitations remain despite additive or curing improvements. The evidence indicates that CFA concretes may still have limitations. For example, one study found that ordinary concrete with 30% CFA showed greater 28-day carbonation than control concrete [N6-R4]. Another found that strength can be directly proportional to water absorption in CFA-concrete systems [N6-R1]. These results suggest that even with additives or improved curing, CFA mixes may retain some weaknesses, such as higher initial porosity, different hydration kinetics, or greater susceptibility to early-age transport processes [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence also suggests that CFA’s durability benefits may be conditional on mix design, exposure, and curing conditions rather than automatic [N5-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5].

Fourth, CFA’s properties interact with additives and microwave curing. CFA’s pozzolanic and permeability-reducing properties make it compatible with additives like nanosilica and metakaolin, which also refine pore structure and improve durability [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. Similarly, microwave curing may enhance early hydration and microstructure refinement, but CFA-specific behavior can determine how effective this is [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5]. In other words, CFA can amplify the benefits of additives and curing, but it can also impose constraints that must be managed through mix design and curing control.

Overall, CFA improves durability by reducing permeability and enhancing long-term strength, but it can also create porosity-related limitations that affect chloride, sulfate, and carbonation resistance [N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R1][N7-R5]. The main CFA-related limitation is that its benefits are conditional: CFA may improve durability, but it may also require careful handling of water absorption, hydration control, and early-age transport resistance [N5-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5][N7-R5]. Its interaction with additives and microwave curing is therefore synergistic in principle, but the exact degree of benefit depends on the baseline CFA mix behavior [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].

The combined effects of microwave curing and nano-additives on CFA cement are generally synergistic, with microwave curing often enhancing additive benefits, improving compressive strength and durability, and the most effective combinations being those that combine early-age hydration acceleration with pore refinement. However, the synergy is not automatic and depends on mix design, additive selection, and CFA-specific behavior.

First, microwave curing often enhances or preserves additive benefits rather than diminishing them. The evidence on microwave curing shows that microwave treatment can accelerate hydration and improve early-age strength, with higher temperatures associated with faster hydration reactions and higher early-age strength [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3]. In the microwave-specific evidence, microwave curing was also described as offsetting early-age strength deficiency in MK mortars and improving 28-day strength [N8-R2]. This is important because many additives, especially pozzolanic ones like nanosilica and metakaolin, may not fully realize their benefits without sufficient hydration and microstructure refinement. The evidence also suggests that appropriately controlled microwave curing provides concurrent improvements in strength, durability-related properties, and sustainability [N4-R5]. So, in most cases, microwave curing appears to support additive performance rather than reduce it.

Second, the combination affects compressive strength and durability positively. The synergy evidence is strongest for nanosilica and metakaolin together. One study found that using metakaolin waste and nano-silica together significantly enhanced the long-term strength of concrete, with the mix showing improved mechanical properties after 2 years [N4-R1]. Another study reported concrete samples with 28-day strengths of 31.5 MPa, 5.7 MPa splitting tensile strength, and 10.6 MPa flexural strength when metakaolin and silica fume were used together [N4-R2]. A third source described geopolymer concrete specimens substituted with 10% metakaolin and 3% nano-silica as having better mechanical properties and improved pore structure observations [N4-R3]. These results indicate that the combination can improve compressive strength, flexural strength, and durability-related microstructure.

The durability benefit is also supported by microstructure evidence. The same synergy evidence notes that modified metakaolin with nano-silica improves mechanical properties and durability [N4-R4]. Additionally, the broader pozzolanic evidence in the upstream aggregates indicates that nanosilica refines pore structure, reduces permeability, and improves durability [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2]. Metakaolin also improves compressive strength and durability, with microstructure refinement and long-term performance being central to its effect [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. In combination, microwave curing, nanosilica, and metakaolin therefore work through complementary mechanisms: microwave curing accelerates hydration and reduces early-age defects, while the additives refine microstructure and pore structure, together improving both compressive strength and durability [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R3][N8-R2][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].
